objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain how the flight instruments show attitude, teach the control-and-performance and primary-and-supporting methods, fly straight-and-level by instruments from the right seat while explaining it, and spot and fix a learner's cross-check, interpretation and control errors.
why: A pilot who has not been trained in attitude instrument flying, or whose skills have eroded, loses control in about 10 minutes once forced onto the instruments [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]. A private pilot applicant needs only 3 hours of training by reference to instruments, and straight and level flight heads the list [[60:300|14 CFR 61.109(a)(3)]], so what you teach in those hours has to stick. Your job is to build a cross-check and a light touch that still work on a dark, hazy night with no horizon.

warmup: Think first: your private pilot learner holds altitude within 30 feet under the hood, but every time you ask for the heading she has to search the panel for it, and twice she pushed the nose down when the airspeed was low because you had quietly pulled the power back. Is this a control problem, a cross-check problem or an interpretation problem, and what would you change in the next lesson?

key_terms.def: Controlling the aircraft's position in space by the instruments instead of outside visual references [[23:134|IFH 6-1]].
Set attitude and power on the control instruments, trim, cross-check the performance instruments, then adjust [[23:135|IFH 6-2]] [[23:136|IFH 6-3]].
Groups instruments by control function (pitch, bank, power, trim) and names the one giving the most pertinent information for each [[23:137|IFH 6-4]] [[23:143|IFH 6-10]].
Show attitude and power immediately and are calibrated for precise adjustments: attitude indicator and power gauges such as manifold pressure, tachometer or fuel flow [[23:135|IFH 6-2]].
Show what the aircraft is actually doing: altimeter, airspeed indicator and VSI [[23:135|IFH 6-2]].
The instrument with the most pertinent information for a maneuver, usually the one to hold at a constant indication [[23:167|IFH 7-6]].
The continuous, logical observation of instruments for attitude and performance information; also called scanning or instrument coverage [[23:143|IFH 6-10]].
Understanding each instrument's construction and operating principles and applying it to the aircraft, the maneuver and the conditions [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].
Staring at a single instrument; it usually happens for a reason but gives poor results [[23:144|IFH 6-11]] [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].
Leaving an instrument out of the cross-check, often by failing to anticipate what it will show after an attitude change [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].
Relying on one instrument, usually the one most readily understood, instead of the combination needed [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].
The delay before the VSI shows a stable reading after a pitch change; it grows with the speed and size of the change [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].

chunks.title: Two ways to teach attitude instrument flying

body.p: In visual flight the pilot controls attitude with reference points on the airplane against the natural horizon. In instrument flight the instruments take over, and read correctly they give essentially the same information [[23:135|IFH 6-2]]. On the attitude indicator the natural horizon is replaced by the artificial horizon [[23:149|IFH 6-16]]. The Private lesson PA.VIII.A covers the pilot's side of this Task; this lesson adds the instructor's side.

The IFH gives two learning methods, "control and performance" and "primary and supporting". Both use the same instruments and the same control responses. They differ only in how much they lean on the attitude indicator and how the other instruments are interpreted [[23:135|IFH 6-2]].

head: Group
Instruments
What they tell the pilot
rows: Control
Attitude indicator; power indicators such as manifold pressure, tachometer, fuel flow
Immediate attitude and power, calibrated so they can be set in precise steps [[23:135|IFH 6-2]]
Performance
Altimeter, airspeed indicator, VSI
What the airplane is actually doing [[23:135|IFH 6-2]]
Navigation
Course, range and glideslope indicators, bearing pointers
Position relative to a navigation facility or fix [[23:135|IFH 6-2]]

body.p: Control and performance, in four steps you can put on a whiteboard:

bullets: 1. Set an attitude and power on the control instruments. Known attitude changes and approximate power settings cut the workload [[23:135|IFH 6-2]].
2. Trim until the control pressures are gone. Hands-off trim is essential for smooth, precise control [[23:135|IFH 6-2]] and frees the pilot for other duties [[23:136|IFH 6-3]].
3. Cross-check the performance instruments. This is seeing and interpreting: if something is off, decide how much and which way [[23:136|IFH 6-3]].
4. Adjust attitude, power or both on the control instruments [[23:136|IFH 6-3]].

body.p: Primary and supporting groups the instruments by control function: pitch, bank, power and trim [[23:137|IFH 6-4]]. For straight-and-level at a constant airspeed the altimeter is primary for pitch, the heading indicator for bank and the airspeed indicator for power [[23:143|IFH 6-10]]. The attitude indicator is still the basic attitude reference and should always be used when available [[23:143|IFH 6-10]].

Function and operation worth teaching: power indicators are not affected by turbulence, poor trim or accidental control pressure, so once power is set it needs little attention. Move the throttle by feel first, then cross-check the gauge, and do not fixate on it [[23:137|IFH 6-4]].

callout.text: Application: pick one method's words for a learner and stay with it. Mixing "set the control instrument" and "the altimeter is primary" in the same lesson without explaining that both describe the same hand movements confuses beginners. The IFH says the control responses are the same either way [[23:135|IFH 6-2]].

check.q: A learner asks why the attitude indicator is called a control instrument but the altimeter a performance instrument. What do you answer?
check.a: Control instruments show attitude and power immediately and can be set in precise steps; performance instruments show the result of that attitude and power [[23:135|IFH 6-2]].

body.p: Pitch attitude comes from the airspeed indicator, altimeter, VSI and attitude indicator. Bank attitude comes from the heading indicator, turn coordinator and attitude indicator [[23:147|IFH 6-14]]. Only the attitude indicator shows the actual attitude both instantly and directly [[23:140|IFH 6-7]]; the others show it indirectly [[23:137|IFH 6-4]].

head: Instrument
How it indicates attitude
What to teach the learner to read
rows: Attitude indicator
Directly: miniature aircraft against the horizon bar, and the pointer on the bank scale [[23:163|IFH 7-2]] [[23:167|IFH 7-6]]
Small bank angles are hard to see, especially if the pilot leans or shifts in the seat; check the scale pointer [[23:167|IFH 7-6]] [[23:168|IFH 7-7]]
Altimeter
Indirectly for pitch, at constant power [[23:164|IFH 7-3]]
How fast the needle moves tells how big the pitch error is [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]
VSI
Indirectly for pitch; a trend first, then a rate [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]
The trend shows at once; the rate needs time to settle (lag) [[23:166|IFH 7-5]]
Airspeed indicator
Indirectly for pitch at constant power: nose lower, speed higher [[23:167|IFH 7-6]]
A fast speed change means a big pitch change [[23:167|IFH 7-6]]
Heading indicator
Indirectly for bank, because in coordinated flight a bank makes a turn [[23:168|IFH 7-7]]
At the same airspeed, a fast-moving card means a steep bank [[23:168|IFH 7-7]]
Turn coordinator
Indirectly for bank: roll rate while rolling, then rate of turn [[23:168|IFH 7-7]]
It shows rate and direction of turn, not a bank angle [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]]

body.p: Interpretation depends on the airplane. In the IFH example, two bar widths nose-up at full power gives about 500 fpm at 90 knots in a small airplane, while the same picture in a jet gives 2,000 fpm at 250 knots [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. For each maneuver the learner should know what performance to expect and which instruments to read [[23:147|IFH 6-14]].

At a constant airspeed there is only one pitch attitude for level flight: a bit nose-high at slow cruise, a bit nose-low at fast cruise [[23:163|IFH 7-2]]. Until the airspeed is steady and that attitude is found, the attitude indicator alone cannot prove the airplane is level; the altimeter, VSI and airspeed indicator confirm it [[23:163|IFH 7-2]] [[23:164|IFH 7-3]].

callout.text: Pitch: attitude, altimeter, VSI, airspeed. Bank: attitude, heading, turn coordinator.

check.q: A learner says the heading indicator is a navigation instrument and has nothing to do with bank. How do you correct this?
check.a: In coordinated flight a bank produces a turn, so the heading indicator shows bank indirectly, and the speed of the card shows how steep the bank is [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].

chunks.title: How each instrument works and how it can mislead

body.p: Interpretation starts with each instrument's construction and operating principles [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. Have the learner look up in the POH what powers each gyro instrument, so a failure does not come as a surprise [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].

head: Instrument
Function and operation
Limitations and potential errors
rows: Attitude indicator
A gyro with a vertical spin axis in a double gimbal; the airplane pitches and rolls around it, and an erection mechanism keeps it upright. Erects in 2 to 3 minutes, up to 5 [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]

Slight nose-up in rapid acceleration, nose-down in rapid deceleration; small pitch and bank error after a 180° turn that clears within a minute or so. Older units tumble past about 60° pitch or 100° roll [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]. On some, the bank scale moves opposite to the bank, so use the miniature aircraft for direction [[1:221|PHAK 8-19]]
Heading indicator
A gyro with a horizontal spin axis, held rigid in space. Not north-seeking unless slaved [[23:114|IFH 5-19]] [[23:115|IFH 5-20]]
Apparent drift of 15° per hour from Earth's rotation: compare with the compass at least every 15 minutes [[23:115|IFH 5-20]]. Worn or dirty bearings make drift worse [[1:222|PHAK 8-20]]
Turn coordinator
Rate gyro canted about 30°, so it senses roll and yaw by precession [[23:116|IFH 5-21]]
Does not sense pitch [[23:117|IFH 5-22]]; shows rate, not bank angle [[1:219|PHAK 8-17]]
Inclinometer (ball)
Balances gravity against the inertia of a turn [[23:115|IFH 5-20]]
Shows only the relationship between bank and rate of yaw [[23:116|IFH 5-21]]. Preflight: full of fluid, no bubbles [[1:220|PHAK 8-18]]
Altimeter
Stack of aneroid capsules sensing static pressure [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]
More than 75 ft off field elevation on the ground: send it for repair [[23:100|IFH 5-5]]. Freezes if the static system blocks [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]
VSI
Rate of static pressure change through a calibrated leak [[23:103|IFH 5-8]]

Lags a few seconds [[23:103|IFH 5-8]]; settles in about 6 to 9 seconds, longer with rough control or turbulence [[1:210|PHAK 8-8]]. If it reads a climb or descent when level, use that reading as zero [[23:166|IFH 7-5]] [[23:167|IFH 7-6]]
Airspeed indicator
Differential gauge: pitot pressure against static pressure [[23:103|IFH 5-8]]
No appreciable lag from the instrument itself [[23:166|IFH 7-5]]. Pitot blocked, drain open: drops to zero; both blocked: acts like an altimeter [[23:98|IFH 5-3]]
Magnetic compass
A bank instrument when used with the heading indicator [[23:140|IFH 6-7]]
Upset by turbulence, climbs, descents, power and airspeed changes; leads and lags in turns [[23:140|IFH 6-7]]

body.p: On glass panels the AHRS sets the horizon line at start-up and the pilot cannot adjust the aircraft symbol [[23:155|IFH 6-22]]. Many light airplanes feed the backup instruments from the same pitot-static sources, so one blockage can affect both displays [[24:364|AFH 18-15]].

callout.text: Teach that every instrument has a failure picture. Comparing the six conventional instruments is how pilots diagnose common failures [[24:364|AFH 18-15]], which is one more reason the cross-check must include all of them.

check.q: Right after leveling off from a long climb and accelerating, your learner sees a slight nose-up on the attitude indicator while the altimeter holds steady. What do you teach?
check.a: Rapid acceleration can give a slight false nose-up that corrects itself within a minute or so [[23:114|IFH 5-19]]. The altimeter and the other pitch instruments catch it, which is why one instrument is never enough [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].

chunks.title: Cross-check techniques and how to teach them

body.p: Cross-check and interpretation are the two fundamental skills. They are learned separately and in a deliberate order, and precision flying is the ability to blend them into smooth control [[23:143|IFH 6-10]]. Cross-checking is mandatory in instrument flight. No single method is recommended: use the instruments that give the best information for the maneuver, hold the important ones at a constant reading, and use the rest to help keep them there [[23:143|IFH 6-10]].

Why it never stops: human error, instrument error and changes in performance with weather and loading make it impossible to set an attitude and have performance stay constant for long [[23:143|IFH 6-10]] [[23:144|IFH 6-11]].

head: Pattern
How the eyes move
Instructor note
rows: Selected radial
80 to 90 percent on the attitude indicator, quick glances out and always back through it [[23:144|IFH 6-11]]
Works well on a PFD, where the attitude display is never out of peripheral view [[23:157|IFH 6-24]]
Inverted-V
Attitude indicator, down to turn coordinator, back up, down to VSI, back up [[23:144|IFH 6-11]]
Keeps bank (turn coordinator) and pitch trend (VSI) tied to the attitude indicator
Rectangular
Across the top row, then the bottom row, either direction [[23:144|IFH 6-11]]
Gives every instrument equal weight, but takes longer to get back to the critical one [[23:144|IFH 6-11]]

body.p: For pitch, the altimeter is the key level-flight instrument except in very strong vertical currents such as thunderstorms. Only the altimeter gives exact altitude, but whichever instrument shows the need, make the change on the attitude indicator [[23:140|IFH 6-7]].

What progress looks like: a beginner scans fast without knowing what to look for. With experience the pilot learns what to look for, when, and what to do about it, and finally cross-checks by habit, matching speed and sequence to the situation [[23:144|IFH 6-11]]. Without regular practice the scan errors come back at any time [[23:144|IFH 6-11]]. On glass panels pilots tend to drop the standby instruments and the compass from the scan [[23:161|IFH 6-28]].

callout.text: Have the learner say the scan out loud for the first few minutes. When the learner thinks aloud you can tell whether an error comes from a misconception or from motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

check.q: Your learner uses the rectangular cross-check and keeps letting the altitude wander. What is the drawback of that pattern for this learner?
check.a: It gives every instrument equal weight and lengthens the time it takes to get back to the instrument that matters most [[23:144|IFH 6-11]]. A pattern that returns to the attitude indicator, such as the radial, may suit better.

chunks.title: Pitch control: teaching a light touch

body.p: Pitch corrections by instruments are much smaller than visual ones, and in a trimmed airplane the pressures needed are very slight [[23:164|IFH 7-3]]. The IFH gives three hints you can turn into coaching lines:

bullets: Relax the grip. A tight grip hides pressure changes, and learning to relax takes real effort early in training [[23:164|IFH 7-3]].
Small, smooth changes with positive pressure, learning to "freeze" a half, one and one-and-a-half bar width [[23:164|IFH 7-3]].

When tense, briefly release all elevator pressure: a trimmed airplane holds level flight except in turbulence. Resisting the urge to move the controls may be one of the hardest early problems [[23:164|IFH 7-3]].

body.p: The bar-width drill: restrict the horizon bar to a half, then one, then one-and-a-half bar widths up or down [[23:164|IFH 7-3]]. The wings and center dot of the miniature aircraft stand for about 2° of pitch [[23:114|IFH 5-19]].

Two demonstrations the IFH gives the instructor: first, make normal pitch corrections and compare the attitude indicator with the airplane's position against the natural horizon [[23:164|IFH 7-3]]. Second, show an excessive nose-down deviation and the wrong fix: a big, hurried correction makes the needle slow, reverse and swing to nose-high, with tension and ever larger control movements. Then show the slower, smoother technique, which gets back to altitude sooner [[23:165|IFH 7-4]].

head: Situation
Technique
rows: Altitude error seen
Correct promptly with light pressure, in two changes: one to stop the needle, one to return [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]
Size of the first change
Half a bar width under 100 ft; a full bar width over 100 ft [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]
Rate of return
About double the error, never more than the airplane's best rate for that speed and configuration; the VSI is primary while returning [[23:166|IFH 7-5]]
Rough air
Average the VSI swings and lean on the less sensitive altimeter [[23:139|IFH 6-6]]; do not chase the needle [[23:166|IFH 7-5]]

callout.text: Practice planned altitude changes with the altimeter alone first, then add the attitude indicator [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]. The learner then sees how fast the needle moves for each bar width.

check.q: On a planned 400 fpm return to altitude, your learner's VSI swings to 800 fpm. What is it called and what do you say?
check.a: Overcontrolling: more than 200 fpm away from the rate wanted [[23:166|IFH 7-5]]. Have her relax the pressure and make a smaller change on the attitude indicator.

body.p: To fly straight, keep the wings level with the horizon in coordinated flight, using the attitude indicator, heading indicator and turn coordinator [[23:167|IFH 7-6]]. The attitude indicator gives pitch and bank in one glance with the least effort, even with its precession errors [[23:168|IFH 7-7]]. Those same errors are why a precise heading check is needed to stay straight [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].

bullets: Heading off: bank no more than the number of degrees to turn, and never more than a standard rate bank. Larger banks need a very high skill level and usually cause overcontrolling [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].
Turn coordinator: keep the miniature aircraft in the scan, correct even the smallest deviation, and use very light pressure [[23:169|IFH 7-8]].
Ball: off center means a slip or skid. Wings level and properly trimmed, the ball stays centered [[23:169|IFH 7-8]].
Ball left and left wing low: left rudder to center the ball, right aileron to level the wings, then retrim [[23:169|IFH 7-8]].

body.p: Power: any power change changes airspeed or altitude. At a given airspeed, power decides climb, level or descent; at a constant altitude, power decides airspeed [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]. Teach the learner to check the altimeter before deciding a power change is needed [[23:169|IFH 7-8]].

When altitude and airspeed are off in opposite directions, pitch alone may fix both; when both are high or both low, pitch and power are needed [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]. Adding power makes the pitch instruments show a climb unless forward pressure is used, and the airplane yaws and rolls left unless aileron and rudder counter it [[23:170|IFH 7-9]]. As thrust comes off, speed up the cross-check and be ready for left rudder, back pressure and aileron [[23:172|IFH 7-11]].

Next step once cruise is solid: airspeed changes in straight-and-level flight develop all three skills and bring out the common errors [[23:172|IFH 7-11]]. Overpower or underpower briefly to speed the change [[23:170|IFH 7-9]], then add gear and flap changes within the POH limits [[23:172|IFH 7-11]]. Proficiency means holding altitude and heading with smooth pitch, bank, power and trim during big attitude changes [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

check.q: Heading is 6° off and your learner rolls into a standard-rate bank to fix it. Is that right?
check.a: No. Bank no more than the degrees to turn, about 6° here; standard rate is the upper limit, not the target [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].

body.p: An airplane is correctly trimmed when it holds the attitude with all control pressures neutralized. How much skill a pilot ends up with depends largely on how well he or she learns to keep it trimmed [[23:141|IFH 6-8]]. With the pressures gone the attitude is easier to hold and there is more time for navigation and other duties [[23:143|IFH 6-10]].

bullets: Set the attitude with control pressure, then trim so it holds when the controls are released [[23:143|IFH 6-10]].
Rudder trim toward the side the ball is displaced, then aileron trim, if fitted, to hold wings level [[23:143|IFH 6-10]].
Changes in attitude, power or configuration usually need retrimming. Using trim alone to change attitude leads to erratic control [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].
With only the turn coordinator: aileron to level the miniature aircraft, rudder to center the ball, hold them, then release slowly while rudder trim takes the pressure [[23:169|IFH 7-8]].

body.p: Trim faults the IFH lists: seat or pedals set so the ankles are tense; confusion about trim devices that differ between airplanes, some turning opposite to what is expected; trimming in place of flying the airplane; too much trim; and not understanding why trim changes [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].

callout.text: For the VFR learner's emergency, the AFH makes trim the first key: elevator trim for hands-off level flight at cruise speed, then resist the urge to overcontrol [[24:367|AFH 18-18]].

check.q: A learner who trained in one airplane rolls the trim the wrong way in your school's other model. Which trim fault is this and how do you prevent it?
check.a: Confusion about trim devices that differ among airplanes, some turning opposite to what is expected [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]. Brief and practice the trim on the ground in each new type.

chunks.title: Risk: distractions, priorities, fixation and omission

body.p: These are the risks you see from the right seat on every hood lesson. Each has a name; teach it by name.

bullets: Distractions: a distraction pulls attention away for a moment; an interruption makes the learner stop one task for another and is a major source of errors [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. Useful distractions include finding a heading on a chart, resetting the clock and computing true airspeed [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

Task prioritization: during an airspeed change learners stare at the power gauge, but a small power error matters less than a large altitude or heading error [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]. When overloaded: stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].
Loss of situational awareness: fatigue, stress and overload can fix a pilot on one item, and many accidents start with a small distraction such as a gauge not reading right [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]].

Disorientation: build a cross-check with little head movement, and pick up dropped items with minimal head movement [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]]. Large corrections with rapid attitude changes can also lead to spatial disorientation [[23:155|IFH 6-22]].

body.p: Fixation, omission and emphasis are the three scan errors [[23:144|IFH 6-11]] [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]:

head: Error
What it looks like
How you spot it from the right seat
rows: Fixation

Staring at an altimeter 200 ft low while tension on the controls lets the heading wander [[23:144|IFH 6-11]] [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. On glass: fixing on trend vectors, or holding airspeed to one knot [[23:160|IFH 6-27]] [[23:161|IFH 6-28]]
A long stare at one instrument [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]
Omission
Leveling from a 180° steep turn on the attitude indicator alone and never checking heading [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. The slip/skid indicator is one of the most often omitted [[23:161|IFH 6-28]]
The gaze never goes to an instrument, such as the engine gauges [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]
Emphasis
Trusting the instrument best understood: the attitude indicator alone holds altitude only roughly [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]
Altitude drifts slowly while the picture on the attitude indicator looks perfect

body.p: Beginning instrument pilots typically fixate on particular instruments, and fixation is often a sign the task has not been practiced enough on its own [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]. Emphasis is common early and becomes a habit if not corrected [[23:161|IFH 6-28]]. Watching the eyes has a limit: looking at an instrument is not the same as seeing it [[25:82|AIH 3-31]].

check.q: On a glass panel your learner holds the airspeed within 1 knot while the altitude drifts 120 feet. Name the error and what you tell her.
check.a: Fixation on the airspeed tape. There is no need to hold airspeed to one knot [[23:161|IFH 6-28]]; the CFI ACS allows ±10 knots for this Task (ACS AI.XI.A.S2). Bring the altimeter back into the scan.

bullets: Failure to maintain VFR: anytime a VFR pilot cannot keep attitude control by the natural horizon it is IMC, whatever the weather, and a genuine emergency [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]. The RMH lists continued VFR into IMC as a loss of control scenario, and continued VFR into low ceilings or visibility as a CFIT cause [[30:22|RMH 3-4]]. VFR into IMC is one of the most common causes of fatal accidents [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

Spatial disorientation: in VMC the eyes usually win over false sensations; take them away and false sensations disorient quickly [[1:428|PHAK 17-6]]. The inner ear cannot sense slight attitude changes or changes at a uniform rate [[24:367|AFH 18-18]]. Leveling after a long turn can feel like a turn the other way, and the pilot may roll back into the turn [[23:72|IFH 3-5]].

Loss of control: an untrained pilot, or one whose skills have eroded, loses control in about 10 minutes [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]. Many hours of VFR flying with the attitude indicator as a reference give a false sense of security [[24:367|AFH 18-18]].

Fatigue: it degrades attention, concentration and coordination; skill fatigue upsets timing and narrows attention to the center of vision [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]. Fatigue also makes disorientation more likely [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] [[23:76|IFH 3-9]]. With acute fatigue, stay on the ground [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]].
Stress: when it exceeds the ability to cope, performance falls off rapidly [[1:434|PHAK 17-12]]. In the cloud the AFH says do not panic and make a conscious effort to relax [[24:367|AFH 18-18]].

Emergency off airport landings: a precautionary landing is a planned landing, on or off an airport, when further flight is possible but unwise, and deteriorating weather is a listed reason. It is generally less hazardous than a forced landing, and a non-instrument-rated pilot trapped by weather who never considers one accepts an extremely hazardous alternative [[24:350|AFH 18-1]].

body.p: Teach disorientation by letting the learner feel it. The IFH and PHAK describe instructor-flown demonstrations with the learner's eyes closed, such as climbing while turning, tilting to one side and reversal of motion. Never fly them at low altitude or without an instructor or appropriate safety pilot [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]]. Even feeling nothing is a useful result, because it shows that bank cannot be sensed [[1:430|PHAK 17-8]]. The goal is more confidence in the instruments [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]].

callout.text: Untrained pilots cannot control the airplane by instruments for any length of time [[24:367|AFH 18-18]]. Make sure the learner understands that hood training does not prepare a pilot for marginal weather or IMC [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

check.q: After her 3 hours of hood time your private learner says she could now handle a little cloud. What do you tell her, from the sources?
check.a: Introductory instrument training does not prepare a pilot for marginal weather or IMC [[25:181|AIH 9-11]], and without regular practice skill erosion begins almost immediately [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

chunks.title: Risk: when to ask for help or declare an emergency

body.p: The AIM sets the trigger early: an aircraft is in at least an urgency condition the moment the pilot is doubtful about position, fuel, weather or anything else that could affect safety. That is the time to ask for help, not after it turns into distress [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. Delay has cost lives [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]].

bullets: Keep the controller told about the weather now and ahead. If a route in VFR conditions to a safe landing exists, a non-instrument-rated pilot should take it rather than ask for a vector into IFR conditions [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].
If VFR cannot be maintained, tell the controller, say there is no instrument rating, and declare a distress condition [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].
Radar help is advisory; responsibility for flying the airplane stays with the pilot [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].
Already talking to ATC on an assigned code: keep it unless told otherwise. Unable to reach anyone right away: squawk 7700 [[34:46|AIM 6-3-1]].

The distress or urgency message: MAYDAY or PAN-PAN, station called, aircraft identification and type, the problem, weather, intentions, position and heading, altitude, fuel in minutes, people on board [[34:46|AIM 6-3-1]].

body.p: Teach that declaring an emergency is a correct reaction, not a failure: ATC then gives priority handling, and 14 CFR 91.3 lets the pilot in command deviate from rules as needed to meet it [[25:24|AIH 1-20]]. If a controller sounds rushed, the pilot may ask the controller to slow down [[24:370|AFH 18-21]].

callout.text: Application: have the learner make the full distress call aloud while holding straight-and-level under the hood. It rehearses the words and is a realistic distraction at the same time.

check.q: A non-instrument-rated learner asks exactly what to tell ATC when the clouds close in. What do you teach?
check.a: Say VFR cannot be maintained, state that there is no instrument rating, and declare a distress condition [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]], then give the message items in order [[34:46|AIM 6-3-1]].

chunks.title: Risk: collision hazards under the view-limiting device

body.p: Under the hood the learner cannot see out, so the whole see-and-avoid job is yours. When weather permits, every pilot must keep watch for other aircraft under IFR or VFR [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]].

bullets: Safety pilot rule: simulated instrument flight needs a safety pilot in the other control seat with at least a private certificate with the right category and class ratings [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]], with adequate vision forward and to each side or a competent observer to help [[60:447|14 CFR 91.109(c)(2)]].

Look out, not in: instructors and safety pilots must guard against preoccupation with teaching and be especially alert in simulated instrument flight, where there is a tendency to look inside too much [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]].

Weather margin: fly hood work only when the weather is good enough to make up for the safety pilot's restricted view and the pilot's attention on the panel, with extra margin near busy airways and airports [[33:258|AIM 4-3-16]].

The device: it must keep the applicant from seeing outside without blocking the examiner's view [[60:225|14 CFR 61.45(d)(2)]]. The CFI ACS appendix asks applicant and evaluator to brief when and how it goes on and comes off.
Who flies: brief the positive exchange of flight controls before the flight [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].
Logging: the learner logs instrument time only while flying solely by instruments in actual or simulated conditions [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)]].

callout.text: Application: the moment you lean over to explain the turn coordinator is the moment you stop scanning. Teach from where you can still see out, and give the learner a "look up" call you will use if you need to take control.

check.q: You spend two minutes pointing at the turn coordinator to explain it during a hood lesson. What collision risk did you create, and what does AC 90-48E say?
check.a: Preoccupation with instruction. Instructors and safety pilots tend to look inside too much during simulated instrument flight and must keep watching for traffic [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]].

chunks.title: Teaching a VFR learner to escape inadvertent IMC

body.p: The AFH does not try to teach full attitude instrument flying; it sends pilots and instructors to the IFH and the ACS [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]. Its emergency goal is not precision, but keeping adequate control until visual references come back. The first steps are: recognize and accept the emergency, keep control, and get help to land safely [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

head: Item
AFH emergency technique for the VFR pilot
Compare: IFH precision technique
rows: Attitude
Trim for hands-off level at cruise; fingertip control; change nothing unless the instruments show a definite need; pitch changes no more than one bar width [[24:367|AFH 18-18]]
Half a bar width under 100 ft, a full bar width over 100 ft [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]
Wings
Keeping the wings level is the main concern; good bank control makes pitch easier [[24:367|AFH 18-18]]
Wings level with the horizon, coordinated [[23:167|IFH 7-6]]
Turns
Smallest practical bank, never more than 10°; turn a few degrees, level, repeat [[24:368|AFH 18-19]]
Bank no more than the degrees to turn, never past standard rate [[23:168|IFH 7-7]]
Climbs
No more than one bar width up, add power, accept whatever speed results; power in steps of 100 rpm; expect a left turning tendency [[24:369|AFH 18-20]]
Planned climb speed and power (not part of this Task)
Descents
Power off in 100 rpm steps, never more than 500 fpm, no more than one bar width below level [[24:369|AFH 18-20]]
Planned descent rate and speed (not part of this Task)
Combined maneuvers
Avoid climbing or descending turns [[24:370|AFH 18-21]]
Taught later as separate Tasks

body.p: One speed for everything: once trimmed at cruise, all turns, climbs and descents are flown at that speed until slowing to land [[24:367|AFH 18-18]]. Searching outside while half-flying the instruments gives poor control and can lead to disorientation and loss of control [[24:367|AFH 18-18]].

Application, a lesson order built on these sources: brief the three first steps on the ground; under the hood trim hands-off at cruise; wings level with fingertips; small turns of 10° bank or less; one-bar climbs and descents; then the radio call from the previous chunk.

callout.text: Unless these tasks are practiced regularly, skill erosion starts almost immediately, and the pilot's confidence soon runs well ahead of real ability [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

check.q: Your learner asks why she should not look for gaps in the cloud while flying the instruments. What do you answer?
check.a: Controlling partly by instruments while searching outside gives inadequate control, which can be followed by spatial disorientation and complete loss of control [[24:367|AFH 18-18]].

body.p: Who may teach it: 14 CFR 61.195(c) requires an instrument rating on the flight instructor certificate for instrument training toward an instrument rating, a type rating not limited to VFR, and the commercial and ATP certificates [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(c)]]. The private pilot's 3 hours [[60:300|14 CFR 61.109(a)(3)]] are not on that list.

head: Stage
What you do and say
rows: Ground

Explain the instrument groups and the primary instruments for level flight [[23:135|IFH 6-2]] [[23:143|IFH 6-10]]; warn that corrections are much smaller than visual ones [[23:164|IFH 7-3]]; get the cruise power and level attitude from the POH [[23:162|IFH 7-1]]; brief the hood procedure and the exchange of controls [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
Before the hood
Set the miniature aircraft for level flight at cruise [[23:138|IFH 6-5]]; demonstrate pitch corrections while comparing the attitude indicator with the natural horizon [[23:164|IFH 7-3]]
You fly, you explain
Explain power settings and attitudes as you fly, in the same order as the briefing; if your demo strays, say so at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]
Learner tells, you fly
The learner calls the scan and the corrections, so you can check understanding before the workload rises [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
Learner flies
Bar-width drill, then altitude corrections with the altimeter alone and then with the attitude indicator [[23:164|IFH 7-3]] [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]; later, airspeed changes [[23:172|IFH 7-11]]
Add load
Distractions only after straight-and-level is solid on its own [[25:81|AIH 3-30]] [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]
Assess
Against standards suited to the learner's stage, looking at each element, not only the overall result [[25:182|AIH 9-12]]

body.p: The standard you will be held to: "Maintain altitude ±100 feet, heading ±10°, and airspeed ±10 knots" (ACS AI.XI.A.S2), while demonstrating and explaining at the same time. Your private learner's standard is "Maintain altitude ±200 feet, heading ±20°, and airspeed ±10 knots" (ACS PA.VIII.A.S2). Hold yourself to the tighter numbers in every demo.

bullets: Build the blocks in order: cross-check and interpretation are learned separately and in a deliberate sequence [[23:143|IFH 6-10]].
Same hands, different reference: no difference in control use is allowed whether outside or instrument references are used [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].
Adapt to the airplane: the IFH techniques must be modified to suit each aircraft, using its POH/AFM [[23:162|IFH 7-1]].

check.q: On your CFI checkride, what straight-and-level tolerances must you hold while you explain?
check.a: Altitude ±100 feet, heading ±10° and airspeed ±10 knots (ACS AI.XI.A.S2).

body.p: For S3 the examiner will fly errors on purpose; name the error, say what you see, and give the fix. The IFH sums up pitch trouble as overcontrolling, improper use of power and not cross-checking the pitch instruments [[23:140|IFH 6-7]]. The detailed lists are on IFH 7-12 and 7-13:

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Miniature aircraft not set for level flight
Wings on the horizon bar, yet the altimeter creeps
After the first level-off, adjust it at normal cruise [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]
Pushing for low airspeed when power is the cause
Nose goes down, altitude is lost, airspeed still low
Speed up the cross-check to include all relevant instruments before any input [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]
Uncaging the attitude indicator out of level flight
False picture after uncaging
Stabilize altimeter, heading and cruise speed first [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]
Not reading the attitude indicator for the existing airspeed
Same picture flown at every speed
Teach one level attitude per airspeed [[23:173|IFH 7-12]] [[23:163|IFH 7-2]]
Late pitch corrections
A 20 ft error left alone
Practice small corrections; tolerated errors grow [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]
Chasing the VSI
Pitch follows every needle swing
Cross-check the other pitch instruments; explain lag [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]
Not holding an established correction
Scan slows while waiting for the airplane to settle
Keep cross-checking and trim off the pressure [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Heading not checked during power or pitch changes
Heading drifts during a speed change
Put the heading indicator in every pass [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Misreading heading changes
Corrections made in the wrong direction
Have the learner say which way to turn before rolling [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Premature rudder in anticipation of heading changes
Skids, ball off center
Coordinated aileron and rudder only when needed [[23:174|IFH 7-13]] [[23:169|IFH 7-8]]
Same heading error repeated
Slight left turn corrected again and again
Find the cause, often a wing-low trim condition [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Abrupt throttle; not leading the airspeed
Speed overshoots, extra power changes
Smooth throttle; set the new power just before the target speed [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Fixation on airspeed or power gauges
Erratic airspeed and power during changes
Return to the full scan [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]
Trim as a substitute for control
Attitude changed with the trim wheel
Hold the attitude with pressure, then trim [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]

body.p: Analyze before you correct. When the learner talks through the scan, you can tell a misconception from a motor-skill problem [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

check.q: Your learner sees the heading drift left and turns further left to fix it. Which listed error is it, and what is your fix?
check.a: Misinterpreting heading changes, so the correction goes the wrong way [[23:174|IFH 7-13]]. Have her say which way the card moved and which way she will turn before she rolls.

scenario.title: Hood work on a hazy afternoon
scenario.setup: You are a new CFI. Your private pilot learner comes in for her second hood lesson in a fixed-pitch trainer with a six-pack panel. She worked a night shift and slept about four hours. Visibility is 4 miles in haze, and the practice area sits under a busy airway between two airports. The plan is straight-and-level under the view-limiting device, with you in the right seat as instructor and safety pilot.

questions.q: Before you go, what do you weigh about her night shift?
questions.a: Fatigue degrades attention and coordination and narrows attention to the center of vision; with acute fatigue the advice is to stay on the ground [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]]. Fatigue also makes spatial disorientation more likely [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] [[23:76|IFH 3-9]]. A ground lesson today is a sound choice.

questions.q: Say she is rested on another day with the same haze. Is 4 miles fine for hood work under the airway?
questions.a: Legal is not the test. The weather must be good enough to make up for the safety pilot's restricted view and the pilot's attention on the instruments, with extra margin near busy airways and airports [[33:258|AIM 4-3-16]]. And you must not get absorbed in teaching while she is under the hood [[16:15|AC 90-48E 17.2]].

questions.q: Under the hood her eyes stay on the altimeter, which reads 150 feet low, while the heading wanders 20°. What is happening and what do you do?
questions.a: Fixation: staring at the altimeter with tension on the controls lets the heading drift [[23:144|IFH 6-11]] [[23:146|IFH 6-13]]. You can spot it by a long stare at one instrument [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]. Bring her back to the full scan and correct on the attitude indicator: a full bar width since the error is over 100 feet, in two steps [[23:165|IFH 7-4]].

questions.q: You quietly reduce power. As the airspeed falls she pushes the nose down. Which error is this?
questions.a: Insufficient cross-check and interpretation of the pitch instruments: low power, not a nose-high attitude, caused the low airspeed [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]. Teach her to check the altimeter before deciding on pitch or power [[23:169|IFH 7-8]].

questions.q: The haze thickens until you can barely see a horizon. What now?
questions.a: If attitude cannot be kept by the natural horizon it is IMC for a VFR pilot and a genuine emergency [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]. Doubt about the weather already puts you in at least an urgency condition, the time to ask for help [[34:28|AIM 6-1-2]]. End the hood work and head for better weather.

questions.q: In the debrief, what do you make sure she takes away?
questions.a: That this training does not prepare her for IMC [[25:181|AIH 9-11]], that skill erosion begins almost immediately without practice [[24:366|AFH 18-17]], and the escape basics: trim, wings level with fingertips, bank no more than 10°, and ask for help [[24:367|AFH 18-18]] [[24:368|AFH 18-19]].

skills.do: From the right seat, fly straight-and-level by instruments while explaining the cross-check, which instrument is primary and why, how each indication is interpreted, and coordinated, light control inputs made on the attitude indicator.
skills.practice: Fly the talk-through aloud under the hood with another applicant as safety pilot, explaining in the same order you fly it [[25:177|AIH 9-7]], and drill the half, one and one-and-a-half bar widths [[23:164|IFH 7-3]].

skills.do: While explaining, maintain altitude ±100 feet, heading ±10°, and airspeed ±10 knots (ACS AI.XI.A.S2).
skills.practice: Practice under the hood with a qualified safety pilot [[60:446|14 CFR 91.109(c)(1)]] and add distractions such as radio calls; correct every small error early, since a 1° error is far easier to fix than a 20° one [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].

skills.do: Analyze and correct common errors: when the examiner pushes the nose down for low airspeed caused by low power, chases the VSI or corrects heading the wrong way, name the error, explain the cause and give the fix.
skills.practice: Learn the IFH 7-12 and 7-13 lists with a "what you see" and a fix for each, and take turns flying them for another applicant [[23:173|IFH 7-12]] [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].

quiz.q: In the control-and-performance method, what does the pilot set first?
options: The performance instruments, then the attitude follows
The navigation instruments, then the power
An attitude and power on the control instruments
The trim, then the pitch attitude
quiz.why: Step 1 is to set an attitude and power on the control instruments that will give the performance wanted [[23:135|IFH 6-2]].

quiz.q: Which instrument shows bank attitude directly rather than indirectly?
options: Attitude indicator
Turn coordinator
Heading indicator
Magnetic compass
quiz.why: Only the attitude indicator shows the actual attitude both instantly and directly [[23:140|IFH 6-7]]; the heading indicator and turn coordinator show bank indirectly [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].

quiz.q: Why should a heading indicator be compared with the compass about every 15 minutes?
options: It is slaved to the compass and picks up its turning errors
It leads and lags in turns just as the compass does
Its vacuum supply weakens over a long flight
Earth's rotation gives an apparent drift of 15° per hour
quiz.why: The gyro holds its position in space while Earth turns 15° per hour, so the displayed heading drifts [[23:115|IFH 5-20]].

quiz.q: What is the drawback of the rectangular cross-check?
options: It leaves out the turn coordinator and the VSI on every pass
Equal weight to all slows the return to the key instrument
It cannot be used on a primary flight display
It keeps the eyes on the attitude indicator too long
quiz.why: It gives equal weight to every instrument, which lengthens the time to get back to the one critical to the maneuver [[23:144|IFH 6-11]].

quiz.q: Which IFH demonstration shows a learner why big, hurried pitch corrections fail?
options: A steep turn under the hood with the power fixed
A nose-down deviation fixed in a rush, then fixed smoothly
A full stall entered while the learner watches only the VSI
A climb at full power with the trim held fixed
quiz.why: The instructor shows an excessive nose-down deviation and the hurried fix that overcontrols, then the slower technique that returns sooner [[23:165|IFH 7-4]].

quiz.q: As power comes off for a slower cruise in level flight, what should happen to the learner's cross-check?
options: Slow it down so the pitch changes stay small
Hold the eyes on the tachometer until the new power settles
Leave it alone; level flight needs no change
Speed it up and be ready for pitch and yaw changes
quiz.why: As thrust decreases, increase the speed of the cross-check and be ready with rudder, elevator and aileron [[23:172|IFH 7-11]]. Staring at the power gauge is a listed error [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].

quiz.q: When is an airplane correctly trimmed?
options: All control pressures neutralized at the desired attitude
The trim indicator sits on the takeoff mark
Some nose-up trim is set for cruise speed
The ball is centered while light back pressure is still held
quiz.why: Correct trim means the airplane keeps the desired attitude with all control pressures neutralized [[23:141|IFH 6-8]].

quiz.q: How does the AIH describe an interruption, as opposed to a distraction?
options: A brief diversion after which attention returns
Any radio call that arrives during a maneuver
An event that makes the learner stop one task to do another
A planned task the instructor adds to the lesson
quiz.why: An interruption is an unexpected event for which the learner suspends one task to complete another, and it is a significant source of errors [[25:81|AIH 3-30]].

quiz.q: A non-instrument-rated pilot in difficulty can reach a safe landing in VFR conditions, or ask for a vector through cloud. What does the AIM advise?
options: Take the vector, since ATC then owns the terrain clearance job
Declare distress first and decide on the route later
Climb on top of the layer and wait for help there
Choose the VFR route over a vector into IFR conditions
quiz.why: Noninstrument-rated pilots should choose the VFR condition rather than a vector or approach into IFR conditions [[34:29|AIM 6-2-1]].

quiz.q: In the AFH emergency technique for a VFR pilot in IMC, what is the most bank to use in a turn?
options: No more than 10°
A standard rate bank
About 20°
The degrees to be turned
quiz.why: Use the smallest practical bank, in any case no more than 10° [[24:368|AFH 18-19]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner holds heading within 2°, but the altitude drifts 150 feet over a few minutes. She says she flies "off the attitude indicator because it shows everything." What error is this?
options: Fixation on the heading indicator
Emphasis on the attitude indicator
Omission of the turn coordinator
Overcontrolling of the pitch attitude
final_quiz.why: Relying on the instrument most readily understood is emphasis; the attitude indicator holds altitude only roughly without the altimeter in the scan [[23:146|IFH 6-13]].

final_quiz.q: You ease the throttle back without telling your learner. As the airspeed decays she pushes the nose down. Which IFH error is this, and what is the fix?
options: Chasing the VSI; average the needle swings in rough air
Late pitch correction; correct sooner and always in smaller steps
Faulty trim sequence; hold pressure first, then retrim
Weak cross-check; scan all relevant instruments before acting
final_quiz.why: Applying forward pressure for low airspeed without noting that low power is the cause is insufficient cross-check and interpretation; increase cross-check speed to include all relevant indications before a control input [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

final_quiz.q: A learner flying a PFD is 300 feet below the assigned altitude. Using the IFH glass-panel rule of thumb, what rate of climb should she aim for?
options: About 600 fpm, double the error
About 300 fpm, equal to the error
About 500 fpm, the cap in that rule
About 1,000 fpm to get back to altitude quickly
final_quiz.why: The glass section says to use a rate twice the deviation, not to exceed 500 fpm: 2 x 300 = 600, capped at 500 fpm [[23:155|IFH 6-22]].

final_quiz.q: During an inadvertent IMC drill your VFR learner needs to climb 1,000 feet for terrain. What does the AFH technique call for?
options: Raise one bar width at most, add power, accept the speed
Pitch for Vy and add full power until level
Make a climbing turn toward lower ground at once
Raise two bar widths and hold cruise airspeed
final_quiz.why: Raise the miniature airplane no more than one bar width and apply power, accepting whatever speed results; maximum power is seldom needed [[24:369|AFH 18-20]]. Combined climbing turns should be avoided [[24:370|AFH 18-21]].

final_quiz.q: On your CFI checkride you are assigned 5,500 feet, heading 090° and 100 knots. While explaining you read 5,580 feet, 101° and 92 knots. Which is outside the CFI ACS?
options: Altitude, at 80 feet high
Airspeed, at 8 knots slow
Heading, at 11° off
None; all are within limits
final_quiz.why: The standard is altitude ±100 feet, heading ±10° and airspeed ±10 knots (ACS AI.XI.A.S2). 101° minus 90° is 11°, past the limit. Fix small errors early [[23:174|IFH 7-13]].

final_quiz.q: After the first level-off at cruise, the attitude indicator shows level wings on the horizon but the altimeter keeps creeping up at constant power. What is the most likely cause?
options: A blocked static port
Miniature aircraft not set for cruise
A vertical speed indicator out of calibration
Heading indicator precession
final_quiz.why: Improper adjustment of the miniature aircraft is a listed pitch fault; after the first level-off, adjust it at normal cruise [[23:173|IFH 7-12]]. A blocked static port would freeze the altimeter instead [[23:98|IFH 5-3]].

final_quiz.q: During a hood lesson ATC gives your VFR learner a quick string of heading and altitude changes, and she starts to rush. What does the AFH say?
options: Comply at once; the controller sees the traffic
Make every turn at a standard rate so she can keep up
Switch off the radio until the airplane is stable
It is reasonable to ask the controller to slow down
final_quiz.why: The controller's urgency is normal concern, but the pilot should not rush into a maneuver that could cause loss of control; asking the controller to slow down is reasonable [[24:370|AFH 18-21]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner arrives after a night shift with four hours of sleep. Which effect of skill fatigue does the PHAK describe?
options: Attention narrows to the center of vision and timing is off
The inner ear becomes more sensitive to slow rolls
Control movements become slower but more accurate
Alertness rises for the first hour, then drops
final_quiz.why: Skill fatigue brings timing disruption and a narrowed perceptual field, with loss of accuracy and smoothness [[1:435|PHAK 17-13]].

final_quiz.q: Visibility is legal VFR but hazy, and the practice area sits under a busy airway. What does the AIM say about simulated instrument flight?
options: Legal VFR minimums are all that is needed, with no extra margin
Enough margin to offset the limited view, more near airways
It is not allowed within 5 miles of any Victor airway or airport
Only an instrument-rated safety pilot may be used
final_quiz.why: Be sure the weather is good enough to compensate for the safety pilot's restricted visibility and the pilot's concentration on the instruments, with more margin near busy airways or airports [[33:258|AIM 4-3-16]].

final_quiz.q: In level flight your learner rolls briskly into a bank. For that moment the turn coordinator's miniature airplane reaches the standard-rate mark although the heading has barely changed. What is it showing?
options: A standard rate of turn
A bank angle of about 15°
A roll rate of about 3° per second
A skid toward the outside of the turn
final_quiz.why: While the airplane is rolling, the alignment marks represent a roll rate of 3° per second; the turn rate shows only after the roll stops [[23:168|IFH 7-7]].

final_quiz.q: A new CFI holds no instrument rating on the flight instructor certificate. Which training may she give, under 14 CFR 61.195(c)?
options: Instrument training toward an instrument rating
The instrument training for a commercial certificate
Training for a type rating not limited to VFR
The 3 hours of instrument training for a private pilot
final_quiz.why: 61.195(c) requires the instrument rating on the instructor certificate for instrument rating, type rating not limited to VFR, commercial and ATP instrument training [[60:346|14 CFR 61.195(c)]]. The private 3 hours are not on that list [[60:300|14 CFR 61.109(a)(3)]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner is 60 feet high and the altimeter needle is still climbing. What is her first control action?
options: Change the attitude just enough to stop the needle
Lower the nose a full bar width at once and hold it there
Roll in nose-down trim until the needle stops
Reduce power to the descent setting
final_quiz.why: Correct promptly with light pressure in two distinct changes: first stop the needle, then return to altitude [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]. Under 100 feet, half a bar width is the rule of thumb [[23:165|IFH 7-4]], and trim alone gives erratic control [[23:173|IFH 7-12]].

final_quiz.q: You plan to demonstrate spatial disorientation to a learner. Which condition do the IFH and PHAK rule out?
options: Having the learner fly it with her eyes closed
Flying the demonstration at low altitude
Using a coordinated 50° bank turn
Having the instructor do the flying
final_quiz.why: These maneuvers should not be attempted at low altitudes or without an instructor or appropriate safety pilot [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]]. Having the learner fly with eyes closed is listed as a very effective variation [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]].

takeaways: Two methods, same hands: control and performance, or primary and supporting. Pick one vocabulary per learner.
Only the attitude indicator shows attitude directly; teach the indirect pitch and bank cues of every other instrument.
Teach how each instrument works and how it fails, so the learner recognizes a failure picture in the scan.
Cross-check and interpretation are learned separately, then blended; watch the eyes for fixation, omission and emphasis.
Light grip, small corrections on the attitude indicator, two-step altitude fixes, and trim off every pressure.
For the VFR escape: trim hands-off, wings level, one bar width, 10° of bank, and ask for help early.
Under the hood the traffic scan is entirely yours, and your demo standard is ±100 feet, ±10°, ±10 knots.
cfi_notes: The IFH gives two bar-width rules. Chapter 6 says one pitch correction on the attitude indicator should not exceed a half bar width, with another half if needed [[23:138|IFH 6-5]]; Chapter 7 allows an initial full bar width for errors over 100 feet [[23:165|IFH 7-4]]. Teach the Chapter 7 rule for straight-and-level and explain that both aim at small corrections.

The sources cap the rate of return differently. The analog section says double the error but never more than the optimum climb or descent rate [[23:166|IFH 7-5]]; the glass section says double the deviation, not to exceed 500 fpm [[23:155|IFH 6-22]]. The AFH emergency descent limit is also 500 fpm [[24:369|AFH 18-20]].

The IFH normally calls the altimeter primary for pitch in level flight but says the choice depends on the airplane, the weather and the pilot [[23:167|IFH 7-6]]; the AFH calls the attitude indicator the primary instrument for emergency attitude control [[24:367|AFH 18-18]]. They serve different goals: precision for the instrument student, survival for the VFR pilot.

Bank limits differ by audience: the IFH limits heading corrections to the degrees to turn and never past standard rate [[23:168|IFH 7-7]], while the AFH limits a VFR pilot in IMC to 10° [[24:368|AFH 18-19]]. Tell learners which rule they are practicing.

The IFH Chapter 7 examples assume a retractable airplane with a manifold pressure gauge [[23:162|IFH 7-1]]. In a fixed-pitch trainer the tachometer is the supporting power instrument [[23:170|IFH 7-9]], so translate the numbers to your POH.

Attitude indicator tumble limits differ by model: the IFH gives about 60° pitch and 100° roll for older units [[23:114|IFH 5-19]], the PHAK 60° to 70° pitch and 100° to 110° bank [[1:221|PHAK 8-19]]. Check the instrument in your airplane.
Watching the learner's eyes finds fixation and omission, but looking is not seeing [[25:82|AIH 3-31]]. Pair it with having the learner say the scan aloud [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

Use distractions only after straight-and-level is solid on its own [[25:81|AIH 3-30]]; the AIH list includes dropping a pencil [[25:180|AIH 9-10]], and head movements can set off the Coriolis illusion [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]], so give that one with the wings level.
gaps: Cruise power, the level-flight pitch attitude in bar widths and trim positions for your trainer come from the POH/AFM and your own flying; the handbooks give only sample airplanes.
No source says how many hood hours beyond the 3-hour minimum a VFR learner needs to be reliable at the inadvertent IMC escape.
The sources do not describe types of view-limiting devices or how to fit them; the CFI ACS only says to brief when and how the device goes on and comes off.
No source describes how the attitude indicator looks from the right seat; the IFH only warns that leaning or shifting in the seat makes small banks hard to read [[23:167|IFH 7-6]].
The IFH and PHAK forbid disorientation demonstrations "at low altitudes" without giving a number [[23:75|IFH 3-8]] [[1:431|PHAK 17-9]].

activities.title: Fixing an altitude error, step by step
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the IFH steps in order, then tap Check.
steps: Apply just enough elevator pressure to slow the altimeter needle
If the needle slows abruptly, ease off some pressure, slowly
Add slightly more pressure to stop the needle: the airplane is level
Relax the pressures carefully while you keep cross-checking

activities.title: True or false: hood work and the safety pilot
activities.intro: Decide whether each statement is true or false.

cards.s: In simulated instrument flight the safety pilot needs at least a private pilot certificate with category and class ratings for the aircraft.
On a practical test, a view-limiting device that also blocks the examiner's outside view is acceptable.
cards.why: False. It must keep the applicant from seeing outside without keeping the examiner from seeing outside [[60:225|14 CFR 61.45(d)(2)]].

cards.s: The AIM says hood practice only needs legal VFR minimums, with no extra margin.
cards.why: False. The weather should be good enough to make up for the safety pilot's restricted view, with more margin near busy airways and airports [[33:258|AIM 4-3-16]].

cards.s: A learner may log instrument time for the whole lesson, including the takeoff she flew visually.
cards.why: False. Instrument time is logged only while flying solely by reference to instruments [[60:230|14 CFR 61.51(g)]].

cards.s: AC 90-48E warns that instructors and safety pilots tend to look inside too much during simulated instrument flight.
The preflight briefing should include how the flight controls will be exchanged.

activities.title: Numbers from the handbooks
activities.intro: Work it out, then type your answer.

items.q: Your learner is 150 feet low and sets up the IFH rate of return, about double the error. Above what VSI reading is she overcontrolling?
items.why: Rate wanted: 2 x 150 = 300 fpm [[23:166|IFH 7-5]]. More than 200 fpm beyond the rate wanted is overcontrolling: 300 + 200 = 500 fpm [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].

items.q: A heading indicator drifts 15° per hour from Earth's rotation. If it is reset every 15 minutes, what is the most it can drift between resets from that cause?
items.why: 15° per hour x 15 / 60 hour = 3.75° [[23:115|IFH 5-20]]. Worn bearings can add more [[1:222|PHAK 8-20]].

items.q: A VFR pilot in cloud must descend from 4,500 feet to 2,500 feet using the AFH limit on descent rate. What is the least time it can take?
items.why: 4,500 - 2,500 = 2,000 feet. The rate should never exceed 500 fpm [[24:369|AFH 18-20]]: 2,000 / 500 = 4 minutes.

items.q: Returning 150 feet at 300 fpm, how many seconds does the correction take once the rate is set?
items.why: 150 / 300 = 0.5 minute x 60 = 30 seconds, using the double-the-error rate [[23:166|IFH 7-5]].

activities.title: Teaching the escape, one decision at a time
activities.intro: You are teaching a private learner the inadvertent IMC escape in a fixed-pitch trainer. The weather is good VMC and you are the safety pilot.

steps.s: On the ground she asks what to do first if she flies into a cloud by mistake.
options: Turn around right away with a steep bank
Look outside for a gap and fly toward it
Recognize and accept it, keep control, then get help
Descend to get below the cloud base
steps.why: The first steps are recognition and acceptance, keeping control, and getting help to land safely [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

steps.s: Hood on. She grips the yoke hard and keeps making small pitch movements.
options: Have her trim for hands-off level at cruise and fly with fingertips
Tell her to hold firmer to damp out the bumps
Take control and end the lesson
Have her watch the VSI closely and match it
steps.why: Trim for hands-off level flight at cruise, fly the attitude indicator with fingertip control, and change nothing without a definite need [[24:367|AFH 18-18]].

steps.s: You ask for a 90° heading change.
options: A standard rate turn all the way
A 30° bank to get it done quickly
Rudder only, keeping the wings level
Bank no more than 10°, a few degrees at a time
steps.why: Use the smallest practical bank, no more than 10°, turning a few degrees, leveling and repeating [[24:368|AFH 18-19]].

steps.s: You simulate rising terrain and ask for a 500-foot climb.
options: Full power and pitch for Vy
One bar width up, power in 100 rpm steps, accept the speed
Two bar widths up at cruise power
A climbing turn back the way she came
steps.why: No more than one bar width up, add power, accept whatever speed results, raising power in 100 rpm steps if needed [[24:369|AFH 18-20]]. Avoid combined maneuvers [[24:370|AFH 18-21]].

steps.s: In the debrief she says she could now fly through a thin cloud layer.
options: Agree, since she held the limits well
Suggest she try it next time with you aboard
Explain this does not prepare her for IMC and skill fades fast
Sign her off for it in her logbook
steps.why: This training does not prepare a pilot for IMC [[25:181|AIH 9-11]], and without regular practice skill erosion begins almost immediately [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].
